chapter.title: Object-oriented design
chapter.summary: Classes that stay easy to change: the pillars, SOLID, and the design patterns that appear in real code and LLD interviews.

lessons.title: OOP pillars and the SOLID principles
lessons.summary: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism done properly, composition over inheritance, and the five SOLID principles with before-and-after code.

parts.label: The four pillars
parts.body:
## What OOP is for

Object-oriented programming organises code around **objects** that bundle **state** (data) with **behaviour** (methods), so that complexity is divided into pieces that can be understood, tested and changed separately. The goal is not "use classes"; it is to **manage change**. Good OO design makes the likely changes cheap (add a new payment method) without rippling through the codebase.

## Encapsulation

Hide the internal representation and expose a small, safe interface. Fields are private; methods enforce **invariants** (rules that must always hold).

```java
class BankAccount {
    private long balanceCents;                       // can't be set to anything from outside
    void withdraw(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0 || cents > balanceCents) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        balanceCents -= cents;                        // the invariant "balance >= 0" always holds
    }
}
```

With public fields, any code can break the invariant. Encapsulation also lets you change the representation (cents to a Money type) without touching callers. Beware useless getters and setters for every field ("anemic" objects): expose **behaviour** (`account.withdraw`), not raw data. Tell, don't ask.

## Abstraction

Expose **what** something does, hide **how**. Callers depend on an `interface` or abstract type (`PaymentGateway.charge`) and never on the Stripe-specific details. A good abstraction is small, named after the domain, and stable. A leaky or premature abstraction costs more than none.

## Inheritance

A subclass reuses and specialises a parent (`Dog extends Animal`). It models an **is-a** relationship and enables polymorphism, but it is the **tightest coupling** OO offers: subclasses depend on the parent's implementation details (the **fragile base class** problem), and deep hierarchies become rigid. Rules of thumb:

- Inherit for a true is-a relationship **and** behaviour substitutability (see Liskov below); otherwise don't.
- Prefer **composition**: give an object a collaborator (has-a) instead of inheriting from it. A `Car` has an `Engine`; it is not a kind of Engine.
- Prefer interfaces to abstract base classes; keep hierarchies shallow (2 levels is plenty).
- Mark classes `final` (or design for extension explicitly).

## Polymorphism

The same call behaves differently depending on the actual object. Callers hold a reference to the abstract type; the runtime picks the implementation (**dynamic dispatch**).

```java
for (Shape s : shapes) total += s.area();   // Circle, Rectangle, Triangle each compute their own area
```

- **Subtype polymorphism**: via inheritance/interfaces (above).
- **Parametric** (generics): `List<T>` works for any T.
- **Ad hoc** (overloading): same name, different parameter types, resolved at compile time.
- Duck typing (Python/JS): any object with the right methods works.

Polymorphism replaces long `if/else` or `switch (type)` chains with objects that know how to do the work, so adding a type adds a class instead of editing a dozen switches.

## Composition over inheritance, concretely

Bad: `class Stack extends ArrayList` exposes `add(index, x)` and `remove(i)` that break stack semantics (Java's `java.util.Stack` made exactly this mistake). Good: a `Stack` class that **holds** a list privately and exposes only `push`, `pop`, `peek`. Likewise, instead of `FlyingSwimmingDuck extends FlyingAnimal, SwimmingAnimal`, give a `Duck` a `FlyBehavior` and a `SwimBehavior` (Strategy pattern) that can vary independently.

## Coupling and cohesion

- **High cohesion**: a class's members belong together and serve one purpose.
- **Low coupling**: classes depend on few others and on abstractions, not concretions.

Almost every design principle is a way to get these two. A useful smell test: if a change forces edits in many unrelated places (**shotgun surgery**), or a class changes for several unrelated reasons (**divergent change**), cohesion and coupling are off.

parts.label: SOLID
parts.body:
## S: Single Responsibility Principle

*A class should have one reason to change.* "Reason to change" means one **actor/stakeholder** whose requirements may change it.

Before: `Invoice` calculates totals, formats a PDF, **and** saves to the database. The accounting rules, the layout designers and the DBA each force edits to the same class.

After: `Invoice` (data and totals), `InvoicePrinter`, `InvoiceRepository`. Each changes for one reason. Don't over-apply: one-method classes everywhere is not SRP.

## O: Open/Closed Principle

*Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.* Add new behaviour by adding new code, not editing tested code.

Before:

```java
double discount(Order o) {
    switch (o.customerType) {
        case REGULAR: return 0;
        case PREMIUM: return o.total * 0.1;
        // every new type edits this method
    }
}
```

After: an interface `DiscountPolicy` with `RegularDiscount`, `PremiumDiscount`, ...; a new customer type is a new class, and `discount()` never changes. Pairs with polymorphism and the Strategy pattern.

## L: Liskov Substitution Principle

*Objects of a subtype must be usable wherever the parent type is expected, without breaking correctness.* A subclass must honour the parent's **contract**: accept at least what it accepts (no stronger preconditions), deliver at least what it promises (no weaker postconditions), and preserve invariants.

Classic violation: `Square extends Rectangle`. Code that sets width = 5 and height = 4 then expects area 20 breaks, because a square's `setWidth` also changes height. Square *is a* rectangle mathematically, but not behaviourally substitutable for a mutable Rectangle. Other smells: a subclass throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`, a method overriding to do nothing, or `instanceof` checks in callers.

## I: Interface Segregation Principle

*Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.* Prefer several small, role-specific interfaces over one fat one.

Before: `interface Worker { work(); eat(); sleep(); }`: a `Robot` must implement `eat()` meaninglessly. After: `Workable`, `Feedable`, and so on. In practice: a service that only reads should receive a `ReadOnlyRepository`, not the full one, so it can't write by accident and is easier to fake in tests.

## D: Dependency Inversion Principle

*High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.* The business logic defines the interface it needs; infrastructure implements it.

Before: `OrderService` does `new MySqlOrderRepository()` and imports a mail SDK. It cannot be tested without a database or changed to another store.

After:

```java
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orders;        // abstraction owned by the domain
    private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderService(OrderRepository orders, Notifier notifier) { this.orders = orders; this.notifier = notifier; }
}
```

Dependencies are **injected** (constructor injection) from the outside (the composition root, or a DI container). Dependency *inversion* (the principle) is about the direction of source dependencies; dependency *injection* is a technique to supply them; an IoC container automates it.

## SOLID in perspective

SOLID are guidelines, not laws. They fight rigidity and fragility, but applying them everywhere early produces needless interfaces and indirection. Follow **YAGNI** (you aren't gonna need it) and the **rule of three**: tolerate duplication until the third occurrence reveals the true abstraction. Other helpful heuristics: **DRY** (one source of truth for each piece of knowledge, which is about knowledge, not identical-looking code), **KISS**, and the **Law of Demeter** (talk to your friends, not to strangers: avoid `a.getB().getC().doIt()`).

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Not a recitation of "S-O-L-I-D", but whether you can **look at messy code and say which principle it violates and how to fix it**, and whether you know when not to apply them.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Explain the four pillars of OOP with an example.

**Model answer.** Encapsulation: a `BankAccount` keeps its balance private and exposes `deposit`/`withdraw` that enforce the invariant that the balance never goes negative. Abstraction: callers depend on a `PaymentGateway` interface and not on a specific provider. Inheritance: specialised types reuse a parent's behaviour (used sparingly; composition is often better). Polymorphism: a list of `Shape`s is summed by calling `area()` and each shape computes its own, with no type checks in the caller.

### 2. Inheritance or composition?

**Model answer.** Composition by default. Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent's implementation, hierarchies get rigid, and subclasses can break the parent's contract. Composition lets me combine behaviours at runtime, swap them (Strategy), and test pieces independently. I inherit only for a genuine is-a relationship that honours the parent's contract, ideally from an interface or a small abstract base.

### 3. What is the Liskov Substitution Principle? Give a violation.

**Model answer.** Any code written against the supertype must keep working when given a subtype. The classic violation is `Square extends Rectangle` with mutable width and height: code that sets width and height independently and expects `width * height` is broken by a square. Other signs: subclasses that throw "not supported", strengthen preconditions, or require callers to check `instanceof`. Fix by restructuring the hierarchy or using composition or immutable value types.

### 4. How do OCP and the Strategy pattern relate?

**Model answer.** OCP says to extend behaviour without modifying existing code. Strategy is a mechanism for that: extract the varying behaviour (discounts, sorting, pricing) behind an interface and inject an implementation. Adding a new behaviour is a new class; the code using it never changes. The anti-pattern it replaces is a growing `switch` on a type code.

### 5. Dependency inversion versus dependency injection?

**Model answer.** Dependency inversion is the design principle that both high-level policy and low-level details depend on abstractions, with the abstractions owned by the high-level side. Dependency injection is the technique of providing an object's dependencies from outside (constructor injection preferred) instead of constructing them inside. DI makes inversion practical and testing easy; an IoC container such as Spring automates the wiring.

### 6. A class has 3,000 lines and 25 dependencies. What's wrong and what do you do?

**Model answer.** It violates single responsibility and has low cohesion and high coupling. I'd write characterisation tests first, then identify clusters of methods and data that change together and extract them into collaborators with narrow interfaces, move incrementally behind the existing API, and let the original class delegate. I would not rewrite everything at once.

### 7. When is it wrong to apply these principles?

**Model answer.** When it adds abstraction without a real variation point: an interface with one implementation and no test seam, or splitting trivial logic into many tiny classes. Principles exist to reduce the cost of change; if there is no change on that axis, simpler code wins. I wait for a second or third use before abstracting.

## Rapid-fire

- **Tell, don't ask?** Put behaviour with the data it needs.
- **Anemic domain model?** Objects with only getters/setters and logic elsewhere.
- **Law of Demeter?** Don't reach through objects (`a.b.c.d()`).
- **YAGNI?** Don't build for requirements that don't exist yet.
- **Constructor vs setter injection?** Constructor: immutable, required dependencies are explicit.

keyPoints: Encapsulation protects invariants, abstraction hides how, inheritance models is-a (use sparingly), polymorphism lets callers depend on abstract types.
Prefer composition over inheritance; aim for high cohesion and low coupling.
SRP one reason to change; OCP extend without modifying; LSP subtypes honour the parent's contract; ISP small client-specific interfaces; DIP depend on abstractions owned by the high level.
Dependency injection (constructor) is the practical way to apply DIP and makes testing easy.
Apply principles to reduce the cost of real change; avoid speculative abstraction (YAGNI, rule of three).

options: Code that sets width and height independently and expects width times height breaks for a square
check.q: Why does Square extends Rectangle (with setWidth and setHeight) violate LSP?
check.why: A subtype must be usable wherever the supertype is expected; mutating one side of a square changes the other, violating the Rectangle contract.

options: Add another case to a switch statement
Add a new class implementing a DiscountPolicy interface
Copy the method and rename it
check.q: Which change best follows the Open/Closed Principle for new discount types?
check.why: A new implementation extends behaviour without modifying tested code that already works with the interface.

options: Explicit required dependencies and easy substitution in tests
check.q: What does constructor injection primarily improve?
check.why: Dependencies are visible and immutable, and tests can pass fakes without a framework or global state.

lessons.title: Design patterns I: creational and structural
lessons.summary: Factory, Builder, Singleton and its pitfalls, then Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy and Composite, each with the problem it solves, a code example and when not to use it.

parts.label: Patterns and creation
parts.body:
## What a design pattern is

A design pattern is a **named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem**, described by its intent, structure and trade-offs. Their value is largely **vocabulary**: saying "wrap it in an Adapter" or "that's a Decorator chain" communicates a design in a sentence. They are not code to copy; they are shapes you recognise. Misused patterns produce over-engineering, so always start from the **problem**.

The classic 23 (Gang of Four) split into **creational** (how objects are created), **structural** (how objects are composed) and **behavioural** (how objects interact; next lesson).

## Creational patterns

### Factory Method / Simple Factory

**Problem.** Callers shouldn't know which concrete class to instantiate, or construction logic varies by input.

**Solution.** Put creation behind a method that returns an abstract type.

```ts
interface Notifier { send(to: string, msg: string): Promise<void> }
function makeNotifier(channel: "email" | "sms" | "push"): Notifier {
  switch (channel) {
    case "email": return new EmailNotifier();
    case "sms":   return new SmsNotifier();
    case "push":  return new PushNotifier();
  }
}
```

Callers depend on `Notifier`; adding a channel touches only the factory (a registry map avoids even that `switch`). **Abstract Factory** produces families of related objects (a UI toolkit's `createButton`/`createCheckbox` for Windows vs Mac). Use when creation varies or is complex; skip when `new X()` is all you need.

### Builder

**Problem.** An object has many optional parameters (telescoping constructors, `new Pizza(true, false, true, null, 3)`), or must be built in steps and validated before use.

**Solution.** A builder with fluent, named setters and a final `build()` that checks invariants and returns an (often immutable) object.

```java
HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.builder().url(u).method("POST").header("A", "b").timeout(5).build();
```

Modern languages also offer named/default arguments, which cover many cases. Builders shine for immutable objects with many options.

### Singleton

**Problem.** Exactly one instance (a configuration, a connection pool, a logger) must be shared.

**Solution.** A private constructor and a static accessor; thread-safe lazy initialisation (in Java, an `enum` or holder-class idiom; in JS/Python a module-level instance already is one).

**Why it is controversial:** it is **global mutable state** in disguise: hidden dependencies, hard to test (state leaks between tests), hard to replace, and trouble with concurrency. Prefer creating one instance at the composition root and **injecting** it. Use a real singleton only for genuinely process-wide, effectively immutable resources.

### Prototype and Object Pool

**Prototype**: create new objects by cloning an existing one (when construction is costly or the class is unknown). **Object pool**: reuse expensive objects (database connections, threads) instead of creating them each time.

parts.label: Structural patterns
parts.body:
## Adapter

**Problem.** An existing class has the wrong interface for what you need (a third-party SDK, a legacy API).

**Solution.** A wrapper that translates calls, so the rest of your code depends on **your** interface. This isolates vendor details and eases replacing them.

```ts
class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
  constructor(private stripe: Stripe) {}
  async charge(amountCents: number, token: string) {
    const r = await this.stripe.paymentIntents.create({ amount: amountCents, currency: "usd", payment_method: token, confirm: true });
    return { id: r.id, ok: r.status === "succeeded" };
  }
}
```

## Decorator

**Problem.** Add responsibilities to an object dynamically, without a combinatorial explosion of subclasses (`CompressedEncryptedBufferedStream`).

**Solution.** Wrappers implementing the **same interface** as the wrapped object, each adding one behaviour and delegating the rest. They stack like layers.

```python
reader = Buffered(Decrypting(Gzip(FileReader("data.bin"))))   # each wrapper adds one concern
```

You meet it everywhere: Java I/O streams, middleware chains, Python function decorators (`@cache`, `@retry`), logging/metrics/auth wrappers around a service. Cross-cutting concerns (retry, caching, tracing) are perfect decorators.

## Facade

**Problem.** A subsystem has many classes and a complex API.

**Solution.** One simplified entry point that coordinates them, such as `OrderFacade.checkout(cart)` calling inventory, payment, shipping and email services. It reduces coupling between clients and the subsystem (but the subsystem remains accessible if needed). Don't let it become a god class.

## Proxy

**Problem.** Control access to another object, with the same interface so clients don't notice.

Kinds: **virtual proxy** (lazy loading expensive objects, e.g. images), **protection proxy** (authorisation checks), **caching proxy**, **remote proxy** (a local stand-in for a remote service: gRPC stubs, RPC clients), **smart reference** (counting, logging). The proxy and decorator look alike structurally; the **intent** differs: a decorator *adds behaviour*, a proxy *controls access* to the same behaviour.

## Composite

**Problem.** Treat individual objects and groups of objects uniformly (file systems, UI trees, org charts, expression trees).

**Solution.** A common interface implemented by both leaves and composites; a composite holds children and delegates to them, so `folder.size()` sums its children and `file.size()` returns its own, and the caller never checks which it has.

## Also worth knowing

**Bridge** separates an abstraction from its implementation so both vary independently (shapes × renderers). **Flyweight** shares common state among many objects to save memory (glyphs in a text editor, interned strings). 

## Choosing

| need | pattern |
|---|---|
| hide which class is created | Factory |
| many optional parameters, immutability | Builder |
| incompatible interface | Adapter |
| add behaviour in layers | Decorator |
| simplify a subsystem | Facade |
| control or defer access | Proxy |
| tree of uniform parts | Composite |

code.source:
# Builder producing an immutable object, validating at build()
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Request:
    url: str
    method: str
    headers: tuple
    timeout: float

class RequestBuilder:
    def __init__(self, url): self._url, self._method, self._headers, self._timeout = url, "GET", [], 5.0
    def method(self, m): self._method = m; return self
    def header(self, k, v): self._headers.append((k, v)); return self
    def timeout(self, t): self._timeout = t; return self
    def build(self) -> Request:
        if self._timeout <= 0: raise ValueError("timeout must be positive")      # invariants checked once
        return Request(self._url, self._method, tuple(self._headers), self._timeout)

req = RequestBuilder("https://api.example.com").method("POST").header("X-Id", "1").timeout(2).build()

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

For LLD rounds: do you **recognise the pattern behind a problem**, name its trade-offs, and avoid forcing patterns where they don't fit?

## Questions with model answers

### 1. When would you use a Factory?

**Model answer.** When the caller shouldn't know or decide the concrete type, or when construction depends on input or configuration, such as choosing an email, SMS or push notifier from a channel field, or a parser from a file extension. The factory returns an abstract type, centralises creation logic and makes adding a type a one-place change. If there is a single implementation and plain construction, a factory is unnecessary indirection.

### 2. Why is Singleton considered an anti-pattern by many?

**Model answer.** It is global state with a nice name: hidden coupling, tests that influence each other, difficulty substituting a fake, and concurrency hazards. I instead create the single instance once in the composition root and inject it, getting the "only one" behaviour without global access. A true singleton remains reasonable for stateless or immutable, process-wide things.

### 3. Decorator versus Proxy versus Adapter?

**Model answer.** All three wrap an object. An adapter changes the interface to what the client expects. A decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour, and can be stacked. A proxy keeps the interface and controls access to the real object: lazy loading, caching, authorisation, or remote calls. Intent is what distinguishes them.

### 4. Where do you see the Decorator pattern in everyday code?

**Model answer.** Java I/O streams (`new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(...))`), HTTP middleware chains, Python decorators like `functools.lru_cache`, and service wrappers that add retry, circuit breaking, caching, metrics or tracing around a client without modifying it.

### 5. How does Builder differ from Factory?

**Model answer.** A factory decides *which* object to create and returns it in one call. A builder constructs *one complex object* step by step with many optional parts, validating before producing an often immutable result. Use a builder for many parameters; a factory for choosing among types. They combine: a factory can return a configured builder.

### 6. Design the classes for a file system with files and folders.

**Model answer.** Composite: an abstract `Node` with `name`, `size()` and `path()`; `File` is a leaf, `Folder` holds a list of nodes and implements `size()` by summing children. Operations like `find`, `delete` and `print` are implemented once on the interface and recurse through folders, so clients treat a file and a folder uniformly. I'd keep parent pointers for `path()` and consider a visitor if many operations get added.

### 7. What is the Facade pattern's main risk?

**Model answer.** It can grow into a god object that knows too much and becomes a dumping ground, and it can hide complexity that callers need to control. Keep a facade thin, orchestrating existing services, and allow direct access to the subsystem for advanced uses.

## Rapid-fire

- **Which pattern replaces telescoping constructors?** Builder.
- **Which wraps a third-party SDK behind your interface?** Adapter.
- **Python's @decorator is the same as the Decorator pattern?** Related idea: wrap a function to add behaviour.
- **Singleton alternative?** Dependency injection of one shared instance.
- **Which pattern fits trees like menus or file systems?** Composite.

keyPoints: Patterns are named solutions to recurring problems; their main value is shared vocabulary, and they should be chosen from the problem, not applied for their own sake.
Creational: Factory hides which class is created, Builder assembles complex immutable objects, Singleton is global state (prefer injecting one instance).
Structural: Adapter converts an interface, Decorator adds layered behaviour, Facade simplifies a subsystem, Proxy controls access, Composite treats leaves and groups uniformly.
Decorator and Proxy have the same shape but different intent: add behaviour versus control access.
Cross-cutting concerns like retry, caching and logging are natural decorators.

check.q: A class from a vendor SDK has the wrong method names and types for your code. Which pattern fits?
check.why: An Adapter translates the vendor interface to the one your code depends on, isolating the vendor details.

check.q: Which pattern lets you stack logging, caching and retry around a service without changing the service?
check.why: Decorators implement the same interface, wrap the inner object and add one behaviour each, so they compose in layers.

options: They are global mutable state that hides dependencies and hurts testing
check.q: What is the usual objection to Singletons?
check.why: Global access creates hidden coupling and shared state between tests; injecting a single instance gives the same uniqueness without those costs.

lessons.title: Design patterns II: behavioural patterns and LLD interviews
lessons.summary: Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method, Chain of Responsibility and Iterator, plus a repeatable method for low-level design interviews with a worked parking-lot example.

parts.label: Behavioural patterns
parts.body:
## Strategy

**Problem.** Several interchangeable algorithms (pricing, sorting, routing, compression), chosen at runtime, currently live in `if/else` blocks.

**Solution.** An interface for the algorithm and one class per variant; the context holds a strategy and delegates. In languages with first-class functions, a strategy is often just a function passed in.

```ts
type PricingStrategy = (basePrice: number, qty: number) => number;
const regular: PricingStrategy = (p, q) => p * q;
const bulk: PricingStrategy = (p, q) => (q >= 10 ? p * q * 0.9 : p * q);
class Cart { constructor(private pricing: PricingStrategy) {}  total(items) { /* uses this.pricing */ } }
```

## Observer (publish/subscribe)

**Problem.** When one object changes, several others must react, without the subject knowing who they are (UI updates, event buses, notifications, data binding).

**Solution.** Subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them on change. Watch for: **memory leaks** (forgetting to unsubscribe keeps observers alive), **ordering** and re-entrancy surprises, exceptions in one observer affecting others, and cascades of updates. Variations: DOM events, `EventEmitter`, RxJS observables, message brokers (the distributed form).

## Command

**Problem.** Turn a request into an object so you can queue it, log it, retry it, or **undo** it.

**Solution.** A `Command` with `execute()` (and `undo()`); an invoker stores a history. Used for editor undo/redo, job queues, transaction logs, macro recording, and as the basis of event sourcing.

## State

**Problem.** An object's behaviour depends on its state, producing sprawling conditionals (`if (status === "pending") ... else if ...`).

**Solution.** Represent each state as a class (or a table of allowed transitions); the context delegates to its current state, which performs the action and decides the next state. Order lifecycle, vending machines, traffic lights, connection states and media players are classic. For many simple cases an explicit **transition table** (`{ pending: ["paid", "cancelled"], paid: ["shipped", "refunded"] }`) is clearer than classes, and it makes illegal transitions impossible to express.

## Template Method

**Problem.** Several algorithms share the same skeleton but differ in some steps.

**Solution.** A base class defines the skeleton (`run(): open(); parse(); validate(); save()`) with abstract steps that subclasses fill in. It's inheritance-based; the composition alternative is passing step functions to a shared routine (Strategy). Frameworks use it widely (lifecycle hooks).

## Chain of Responsibility

**Problem.** A request may be handled by one of several handlers, which should not be hard-wired.

**Solution.** Handlers linked in a chain; each handles the request or passes it on. Middleware pipelines (Express, servlet filters), approval workflows (manager → director → VP), logging levels and validation stacks.

## Iterator

**Problem.** Traverse a collection without exposing its structure. Built into most languages (`for...of`, generators, `Iterator`). Implement it yourself when exposing a tree or paginated API as a uniform sequence.

## Others to recognise

**Visitor** adds operations to an object structure without changing its classes (compilers, ASTs); **Mediator** centralises communication between components (chat room, air-traffic control); **Memento** captures and restores state (snapshots for undo); **Specification** composes business rules.

## Choosing

| smell | pattern |
|---|---|
| `switch` on a type choosing an algorithm | Strategy |
| objects must react to another's changes | Observer |
| need undo, queue, log of requests | Command |
| behaviour changes with `status` field | State |
| same steps, different details | Template Method |
| pipeline where any handler may stop the request | Chain of Responsibility |

parts.label: LLD interviews
Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

LLD interviews measure **structured thinking and judgement**: requirements first, then entities, then well-placed patterns, with code that works and is extensible.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Strategy versus State?

**Model answer.** Both delegate to an interchangeable object, but intent differs. With Strategy, the client chooses an algorithm and it stays fixed unless changed from outside (pricing rule). With State, the object's behaviour changes as its own internal state changes and the state objects typically trigger transitions themselves (an order moving from pending to paid to shipped). Strategies are independent of each other; states know their successors.

### 2. How would you implement undo/redo?

**Model answer.** Command pattern: each action is an object with `execute` and `undo`. An invoker keeps an undo stack and a redo stack; running a new command clears the redo stack. For cheap, state-based cases a Memento (snapshot) can be used instead. Commands can also be serialised for logging or replay.

### 3. What problems come with the Observer pattern?

**Model answer.** Memory leaks if observers are never unsubscribed, unpredictable ordering, re-entrancy (an observer modifying the subject during notification), an exception in one listener stopping the rest, and hard-to-trace cascades. Mitigate by returning unsubscribe handles, copying the listener list before iterating, isolating failures, and keeping handlers small; for cross-service events use a broker with idempotent consumers.

### 4. Design a parking lot. Walk me through your approach.

**Model answer.** I clarify requirements (vehicle types, floors, pricing, gates, payments, concurrency), then list entities: `ParkingLot`, `Floor`, `Spot`, `Vehicle`, `Ticket`, `PricingStrategy`, `SpotAllocationStrategy`. Vehicle types and spot compatibility are modelled with enums and polymorphism where behaviour differs. Allocation and pricing are strategies since they will vary. `park()` finds a spot via the strategy and atomically claims it, issuing a ticket; `unpark()` computes the fee and frees the spot. I handle full-lot and double-exit cases, make spot claiming thread-safe, and discuss extensions like EV spots or reservations that add classes instead of changing existing ones.

### 5. How would you design a rate limiter class?

**Model answer.** Define a `RateLimiter` interface with `allow(key)`; implement algorithms as strategies (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket), with per-key state in a map guarded by locks or atomic operations, a clock abstraction for testing, and eviction of idle keys. A factory builds the configured implementation, and decorators can add metrics. For distributed use the state moves to Redis with an atomic Lua script.

### 6. When does a state machine beat a pile of if statements?

**Model answer.** When there are more than two or three statuses with rules about which transitions are legal. A transition table or state classes make the legal moves explicit and testable, prevent illegal transitions by construction, and give one place to attach side effects such as notifications. The flags-and-conditionals alternative drifts into inconsistent combinations.

## Rapid-fire

- **Which pattern for middleware pipelines?** Chain of Responsibility.
- **Template Method versus Strategy?** Inheritance of steps versus composition of an algorithm.
- **Which pattern for pluggable pricing rules?** Strategy.
- **First step in an LLD interview?** Clarify requirements and scope.
- **How to make `park()` thread-safe?** Atomically claim the spot (lock or CAS) and retry.

keyPoints: Strategy swaps algorithms, Observer broadcasts changes, Command makes actions objects (queue, log, undo), State replaces status conditionals, Template Method fixes a skeleton, Chain of Responsibility builds pipelines.
Observer needs unsubscribe handles and failure isolation; State machines are clearest as explicit transition tables.
LLD method: clarify requirements, list entities and behaviours, relationships, patterns only where variation exists, code the core flow, handle concurrency and edge cases, discuss extensions.
Avoid god classes, pattern overload and untestable hidden dependencies; narrate trade-offs.
Adding a vehicle type or pricing rule should mean adding a class, not editing many.

check.q: In an order lifecycle where legal transitions depend on the current status, which pattern is most appropriate?
check.why: Behaviour and allowed transitions vary with the current state, which the State pattern or a transition table models explicitly.

options: Command encapsulates a request (with undo/queue/log), Strategy encapsulates an interchangeable algorithm
check.q: What is the key difference between Command and Strategy?
check.why: Commands reify an action to store, replay or undo it; strategies are alternative ways to perform one operation chosen by the context.

options: Atomically claiming the spot (lock or compare-and-set) and retrying if it was lost
check.q: Two threads try to park in the last free spot. What prevents both succeeding?
check.why: The check-and-occupy must be a single atomic operation; the loser then picks another spot or reports a full lot.
